title: Blade of the Moon Princess
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: A loose retelling of the Tale of the Bamboo Cutter: Kaguya Takenouchi, a defiant 14-year-old princess of a lunar civilization, is sent to Earth with the sacred sword Futsunuji when the rival Umenouchi line attempts a takeover while her mother the empress is gravely ill. Amid terrorist attacks, she learns to take up her responsibilities to her people. An early work by Tatsuya Endo, released in English by Viz in 2023.
life_message: Real freedom comes with accepting responsibility for the people who depend on you.

content.note: Sword fights, fistfights and terrorist bombings; no on-page deaths in vol. 1 (SKJAM; MU Swordsman, Female Fighter; Viz blurb terrorist attacks).
Coup and terrorism plot with a gravely ill mother.
Obscured bath nudity of the 14-year-old lead and a guard's flirting (SKJAM); MangaDex safe. Single source (to verify).
Kaguya resents being born a princess (MU description).
Defiance of elders as starting point, later outgrown.

dominant: Duty and succession; rebellion versus responsibility; fairy-tale action comedy

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Swordfights and royal honor at stake in the succession struggle.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Kaguya's wish to 'enjoy life' gives way to duty (MU).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Imperial succession and sacred treasures structure the world.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Folktale tradition and sacred regalia (Three Sacred Treasures).

folkways.japan: Built on the Taketori Monogatari folktale and imperial succession with sacred treasures, echoing Japanese court tradition.

delivery.evidence: SKJAM review finds no clear underlying message; duty arc carried by plot per Viz blurb.

personified.ideology: revolution in the name of freedom and equality

delivery.note: The princess's growth into duty is shown through action; revolutionaries are presented as destructive.

winners_losers: Kaguya grows into her royal role; the usurping Umenouchi and the Tengu Revolution are opponents.
to_verify: Strawman call rests on one review: SKJAM says the Tengu Revolution 'claims to fight for freedom and equality but mostly causes destruction'; check with a second source.

Violence in later volumes; review notes no on-page deaths in volume 1.
